subject: chemistry
title: Unit 4 practice exam
summary: A 90-minute practice exam for the whole of Unit 4: six short-answer questions with full worked solutions on organic pathways, spectroscopy, HPLC, food energy, proteins and the practical, plus 20 multiple-choice questions.
body:
This practice exam covers the whole of VCE Chemistry Unit 4. It has six short-answer questions worth 45 marks, followed by 20 multiple-choice questions. Sit it under real conditions so you find out what you actually know, not what you can look up.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 90 minutes in total. Aim for about 25 minutes on the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 65 minutes on the short-answer questions.
- **Conditions:** work alone, with no notes. You may use a scientific calculator and the VCE Chemistry data book (IR, NMR and energy values are all in it).
- Write your short-answer responses on paper **before** you read the worked solutions. Show working, units and significant figures, and draw structures clearly.
- Answer the multiple-choice questions at the end of this lesson. Each one gives an explanation after you answer.
- Mark yourself strictly against the worked solutions, and list every topic where you dropped marks so you can go back to that lesson.

Molar masses used: C 12.0, H 1.0, O 16.0 g mol⁻¹.

## Topics covered

- Naming organic compounds and isomers (structural, cis/trans and optical)
- Organic reactions: addition, substitution, oxidation, condensation and hydrolysis
- Reaction pathways, yield, atom economy and green chemistry
- IR spectroscopy, ¹³C and ¹H NMR, and mass spectrometry
- Chromatography: TLC and HPLC, with calibration curves
- Carbohydrates, proteins and fats; vitamins and enzymes
- Energy from food and calorimetry
- The practical investigation: variables, errors and validity

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (9 marks)

Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, is a solvent used in nail polish remover. It can be made from ethene by the pathway below, where ethene is the only carbon source.

ethene → compound X → compound Y; then X + Y → ethyl ethanoate

a) Name compounds X and Y, and give the reagent and conditions for each of the three reactions. (4 marks)

b) Calculate the atom economy of the final step, given `CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃CH₂OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(l) + H₂O(l)`. (2 marks)

c) A student reacts 6.00 g of ethanoic acid with excess ethanol and collects 6.16 g of ethyl ethanoate. Calculate the percentage yield. (2 marks)

d) Give one reason, other than loss during transfer, why this yield is less than 100%. (1 mark)

### Question 2 (8 marks)

An unknown compound, Z, contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The following data were collected.

- Mass spectrum: molecular ion at m/z 74; other peaks at m/z 45 and m/z 29.
- IR spectrum: a very broad absorption from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong, sharp absorption at about 1710 cm⁻¹.
- ¹³C NMR spectrum: 3 signals, one of them at about 180 ppm.
- ¹H NMR spectrum: a triplet (integration 3) at about 1.1 ppm, a quartet (integration 2) at about 2.4 ppm and a singlet (integration 1) at about 11.5 ppm.

a) What functional group is shown by the IR spectrum? Explain. (2 marks)

b) Identify the ions responsible for the peaks at m/z 45 and m/z 29. (2 marks)

c) Explain what the ¹H NMR triplet and quartet tell you. (2 marks)

d) Give the semi-structural formula and IUPAC name of Z, and name an isomer of Z that would NOT show the broad IR absorption. (2 marks)

### Question 3 (7 marks)

The caffeine content of an energy drink is measured by HPLC. The column has a non-polar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase. Standard caffeine solutions gave these results:

| Caffeine concentration (mg L⁻¹) | Peak area (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|
| 20.0 | 150 |
| 40.0 | 300 |
| 60.0 | 450 |
| 80.0 | 600 |

A 10.0 mL sample of the drink was diluted to 100.0 mL with water. The diluted sample gave a caffeine peak with an area of 270 at the same retention time as the standards.

a) Explain how the caffeine peak in the drink was identified. (1 mark)

b) Calculate the concentration of caffeine in the original drink, in mg L⁻¹. (3 marks)

c) Calculate the mass of caffeine in one 250 mL can of the drink. (1 mark)

d) A second, more polar compound in the drink is also detected. Predict whether its retention time will be shorter or longer than caffeine's, and explain. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (8 marks)

A bomb calorimeter is used to measure the energy content of a peanut.

The calorimeter is first calibrated: a heater running at 4.50 V and 2.20 A for 180 s raises the temperature by 0.540 °C. A 0.800 g sample of peanut is then burned completely in the same calorimeter, and the temperature rises by 5.85 °C.

a) Calculate the calibration factor of the calorimeter. (2 marks)

b) Calculate the energy content of the peanut in kJ g⁻¹. (2 marks)

c) Peanuts are mainly fat. Explain, with reference to their structure, why fats release more energy per gram than carbohydrates. (2 marks)

d) Glucose combustion and cellular respiration have the same overall equation. Give two differences in the way energy is released. (2 marks)

### Question 5 (8 marks)

Glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) and alanine (H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH) can react to form a dipeptide.

a) Write the semi-structural formula of the dipeptide formed when the –COOH of glycine reacts with the –NH₂ of alanine, and name the type of reaction. (2 marks)

b) Name the bond formed, and state which level of protein structure it defines. (2 marks)

c) Alanine has a chiral centre but glycine does not. Explain. (2 marks)

d) The enzyme pepsin works best at about pH 2. Explain why its activity drops sharply at pH 8. (2 marks)

### Question 6 (5 marks)

For her practical investigation, a student asks: "How does the temperature of the electrolyte affect the voltage of a hydrogen fuel cell?" She measures the voltage at five temperatures using a digital voltmeter.

a) Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and two controlled variables. (2 marks)

b) Her voltmeter reads 0.05 V too high at every measurement. Name this type of error and state whether it affects accuracy or precision. (2 marks)

c) Suggest how she could improve the reliability of her results. (1 mark)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a)
- X is **ethanol** and Y is **ethanoic acid**. (1 mark for both names)
- Step 1: ethene + steam, with a **phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) catalyst**, at about 300 °C and high pressure (addition/hydration). (1 mark)
- Step 2: ethanol is oxidised by **acidified potassium dichromate (Cr₂O₇²⁻/H⁺)** or acidified permanganate, heated under reflux (oxidation). (1 mark)
- Step 3: ethanol + ethanoic acid, with a few drops of **concentrated sulfuric acid** as catalyst, heated under reflux (condensation/esterification). (1 mark)

b) Molar masses: CH₃COOH = 2(12.0) + 4(1.0) + 2(16.0) = 60.0 g mol⁻¹; CH₃CH₂OH = 46.0 g mol⁻¹; CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ (C₄H₈O₂) = 4(12.0) + 8(1.0) + 2(16.0) = 88.0 g mol⁻¹.

Atom economy = 88.0 ÷ (60.0 + 46.0) × 100 = 88.0 ÷ 106.0 × 100 = **83.0%**

c) n(CH₃COOH) = 6.00 ÷ 60.0 = 0.100 mol. The mole ratio is 1 : 1, so the theoretical n(ester) = 0.100 mol.

Theoretical mass = 0.100 × 88.0 = 8.80 g

Percentage yield = 6.16 ÷ 8.80 × 100 = **70.0%**

d) Esterification is a **reversible** reaction that reaches equilibrium, so not all the acid is converted to ester. (Side reactions or incomplete reaction in the time allowed are also accepted.)

### Question 2

a) A **carboxylic acid** group (–COOH) (1 mark). The very broad band from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid (broadened by hydrogen bonding), and the strong, sharp band at about 1710 cm⁻¹ is a C=O. Both together indicate –COOH (1 mark).

b) m/z 45 is **COOH⁺** (1 mark); m/z 29 is **C₂H₅⁺** (CH₃CH₂⁺) (1 mark).

c) The triplet (3H) is a CH₃ next to a carbon with 2 H (2 + 1 = 3 lines); the quartet (2H) is a CH₂ next to a carbon with 3 H (3 + 1 = 4 lines) (1 mark). Together they show an **ethyl group, –CH₂CH₃** (1 mark).

d) Z is **CH₃CH₂COOH, propanoic acid** (1 mark). Check: C₃H₆O₂ has M = 3(12.0) + 6(1.0) + 2(16.0) = 74.0, matching M⁺; it has 3 carbon environments, with the C=O carbon near 180 ppm; the singlet at 11.5 ppm is the –COOH hydrogen. An isomer with no O–H is **methyl ethanoate**, CH₃COOCH₃ (or ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃) (1 mark).

### Question 3

a) The caffeine peak in the drink had the **same retention time** as the caffeine standards, measured under identical conditions (same column, mobile phase, flow rate and temperature).

b) The calibration line passes through the origin with a gradient of 150 ÷ 20.0 = 7.50 area units per mg L⁻¹ (check: 600 ÷ 80.0 = 7.50).

Concentration of the diluted sample = 270 ÷ 7.50 = 36.0 mg L⁻¹ (1 mark; this lies within the range of the standards)

Dilution factor = 100.0 mL ÷ 10.0 mL = 10.0 (1 mark)

Concentration in the original drink = 36.0 × 10.0 = **360 mg L⁻¹** (1 mark)

c) m = c × V = 360 mg L⁻¹ × 0.250 L = **90.0 mg**

d) **Shorter** retention time (1 mark). The stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase is polar. A more polar compound is attracted less strongly to (adsorbs less onto) the non-polar stationary phase and dissolves better in the polar mobile phase, so it is carried through the column faster (1 mark).

### Question 4

a) E = VIt = 4.50 V × 2.20 A × 180 s = 1782 J (1 mark)

CF = E ÷ ΔT = 1782 J ÷ 0.540 °C = **3.30 × 10³ J °C⁻¹** (3.30 kJ °C⁻¹) (1 mark)

b) q = CF × ΔT = 3300 J °C⁻¹ × 5.85 °C = 19 305 J = 19.3 kJ (1 mark)

Energy content = 19.3 kJ ÷ 0.800 g = **24.1 kJ g⁻¹** (1 mark)

(This is lower than the 37 kJ g⁻¹ for pure fat, because peanuts also contain protein, carbohydrate and water.)

c) Fats are mostly long hydrocarbon chains with many C–H and C–C bonds and very few oxygen atoms, whereas carbohydrates contain about one O atom per C atom (1 mark). Carbohydrates are therefore already partly oxidised; fats are less oxidised, so each gram can react with more oxygen and form more CO₂ and H₂O, releasing more energy (1 mark).

d) Any two: respiration releases energy slowly in many small steps, while combustion is a single rapid reaction; respiration is catalysed by enzymes; respiration occurs at body temperature (about 37 °C), not in a hot flame; in respiration part of the energy is captured in molecules the cell can use (ATP), while combustion releases it mainly as heat and light.

### Question 5

a) `H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH` (1 mark). This is a **condensation** reaction; a water molecule is released (1 mark).

b) A **peptide bond** (an amide bond, –CO–NH–) (1 mark). The sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds is the **primary structure** (1 mark).

c) In alanine, the central carbon is bonded to four different groups: –H, –NH₂, –COOH and –CH₃, so it is a chiral centre (1 mark). In glycine the central carbon is bonded to two H atoms, so two of its groups are the same and it cannot be chiral (1 mark).

d) At pH 8, acidic and basic side chains change their charges (for example –COOH groups lose H⁺ to become –COO⁻) (1 mark). This disrupts the ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure, and changes the shape and charges of the active site, so the substrate no longer binds well and the enzyme may be denatured (1 mark).

### Question 6

a) Independent variable: **temperature of the electrolyte**. Dependent variable: **voltage of the cell** (1 mark). Controlled variables (any two): type and concentration of electrolyte, gas flow rate or pressure, electrode material and surface area, the same voltmeter, the time allowed before reading (1 mark).

b) A **systematic error** (1 mark). It affects **accuracy**, because every reading is shifted from the true value by the same amount; precision is not affected (1 mark).

c) Take repeat measurements at each temperature (at least three) and calculate the mean; the student could also check the voltmeter against a reference or calibrate it to remove the systematic error.

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: The longest chain containing the –OH carbon has three carbons, numbered from the –OH end: the –OH is on C1 and a methyl branch is on C2, giving 2-methylpropan-1-ol. Option C would need the –OH on the branched carbon. Option B would need an unbranched four-carbon chain.

questions.prompt: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₉Cl?
questions.explanation: There are four: 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Students who only count the straight chain get 2; the branched chain (2-methylpropane) adds two more positions.

questions.prompt: Which of these molecules contains a chiral centre?
questions.explanation: In 2-chlorobutane, C2 is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃: four different groups. In 2-chloropropane, C2 carries two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not chiral, which is why it is a tempting wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Which compound is a functional group isomer of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: Methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃, has the same molecular formula (C₃H₆O₂) but is an ester, not an acid. Propanal is C₃H₆O (one fewer O), and ethyl ethanoate is C₄H₈O₂ (one more carbon), so neither is an isomer.

questions.prompt: What is the product when but-2-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide?
questions.explanation: Addition across the C=C puts H on one carbon and Br on the other. Because but-2-ene is symmetrical, both ways give 2-bromobutane. Option C would form from Br₂, not HBr.

questions.prompt: Butan-2-ol is heated with excess acidified potassium permanganate. What is the organic product?
questions.explanation: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, which is oxidised to a ketone, butan-2-one, and no further. Butanoic acid (option A) comes from a primary alcohol, butan-1-ol. Only tertiary alcohols give no reaction.

questions.prompt: Which reagent converts chloroethane into ethanamine?
questions.explanation: Ammonia substitutes for the chlorine to give the amine, CH₃CH₂NH₂. Aqueous NaOH (option A) also causes substitution, but it replaces Cl with –OH, giving ethanol.

questions.prompt: Which change to the production of ethanol best follows the green chemistry principle of using renewable feedstocks?

options.A: Making ethanol by fermenting sugar cane instead of by hydrating ethene from crude oil
options.B: Using a higher pressure to increase the rate of hydration of ethene
options.C: Using concentrated sulfuric acid to dry the ethanol

questions.explanation: Sugar cane is grown again each year, so it is a renewable feedstock; ethene comes from crude oil, which is not renewable. Options B and D increase energy use, which goes against the principle of energy efficiency.

questions.prompt: An IR spectrum shows a strong, sharp absorption at about 1715 cm⁻¹ but no absorption between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹ other than C–H peaks near 3000 cm⁻¹. Which compound could it be?
questions.explanation: The 1715 cm⁻¹ band shows C=O, and the absence of a broad band shows there is no O–H. Propanone has C=O and no O–H. Propanoic acid (option B) has C=O but would also show a very broad O–H from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹.

questions.prompt: How many signals appear in the ¹H NMR spectrum of methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃?
questions.explanation: The two CH₃ groups are in different environments: one is attached to the C=O and one to the O. That gives 2 signals, both singlets, because neither CH₃ has hydrogens on a neighbouring carbon. Option A wrongly treats the two CH₃ groups as identical.

questions.prompt: In the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-chloropropane, CH₃CHClCH₃, the signal for the CH₃ hydrogens is:
questions.explanation: Each CH₃ is next to the CH carbon, which has one hydrogen, so n = 1 and the signal splits into 1 + 1 = 2 lines (a doublet). The septet (option D) is the CH signal, which has 6 neighbouring hydrogens.

questions.prompt: The mass spectrum of propanone, CH₃COCH₃, has a molecular ion at m/z 58 and a large peak at m/z 43. The peak at m/z 43 is caused by:

options.A: the CH₃CO⁺ ion, formed when a CH₃ group breaks off

questions.explanation: 58 − 15 = 43, so the molecular ion has lost a CH₃ group, leaving the CH₃CO⁺ ion. Only positive ions are detected, so the neutral CH₃ piece (option B) never appears. A CH₃⁺ ion (option D) would appear at m/z 15.

questions.prompt: In an HPLC column with a non-polar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase, which component would have the longest retention time?

options.C: the component present in the largest amount
options.D: the component with the smallest peak area

questions.explanation: The least polar component is attracted most strongly to the non-polar stationary phase and dissolves least in the polar mobile phase, so it takes longest to leave the column. The amount present affects peak area, not retention time.

questions.prompt: A juice sample is diluted by a factor of 5 before HPLC analysis. The calibration curve shows that peak area = 50 × concentration (in mg L⁻¹). The diluted sample gives a peak area of 900. What is the concentration in the original juice?
questions.explanation: Concentration in the diluted sample = 900 ÷ 50 = 18 mg L⁻¹. The original juice was 5 times more concentrated: 18 × 5 = 90 mg L⁻¹. Option A forgets the dilution factor, a common way to lose marks.

questions.prompt: Complete hydrolysis of sucrose produces:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose joined by a glycosidic bond; hydrolysis breaks that bond using one water molecule. Two glucose units make maltose (option A), and glucose with galactose makes lactose (option B).

questions.prompt: How many water molecules are released when three amino acids join to form a tripeptide?
questions.explanation: Three amino acids are joined by two peptide bonds, and each condensation releases one water molecule, so 2 water molecules are released. Option B counts the amino acids rather than the bonds.

questions.prompt: The secondary structure of a protein (α-helices and β-pleated sheets) is held in place by:

options.A: disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains
options.B: covalent peptide bonds between amino acids
options.C: ionic bonds between charged side chains
options.D: hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone

questions.explanation: Secondary structure comes from regular hydrogen bonding between backbone C=O and N–H groups. Disulfide bridges and ionic bonds between side chains (options A and C) hold the tertiary structure, and peptide bonds define the primary structure.

questions.prompt: Why is vitamin C water-soluble while vitamin D is fat-soluble?

options.A: Vitamin C is an ionic compound and vitamin D is covalent.
options.B: Vitamin C has many –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water; vitamin D is mostly non-polar with only one –OH.
options.C: Vitamin D has more oxygen atoms than vitamin C.
options.D: Vitamin C is a larger molecule than vitamin D.

questions.explanation: Vitamin C (C₆H₈O₆) is small with four –OH groups, so it forms many hydrogen bonds with water. Vitamin D (C₂₇H₄₄O) is large and mostly hydrocarbon, so dispersion forces dominate and it dissolves in fats. Both are covalent molecules, so option A is wrong, and vitamin D is the larger molecule.

questions.prompt: A 25.0 g snack contains 40% fat, 50% carbohydrate and 10% protein by mass. Using data-book values, what is its energy content?
questions.explanation: Fat: 10.0 g × 37 = 370 kJ. Carbohydrate: 12.5 g × 16 = 200 kJ. Protein: 2.50 g × 17 = 42.5 kJ. Total = 612.5 kJ, or 613 kJ. Option B assumes the whole 25.0 g is fat (25.0 × 37).

questions.prompt: A student's thermometer reads 0.5 °C too high in every measurement. Which statement is correct?

options.A: This is a random error that reduces precision; more repeats will fix it.
options.B: This is a systematic error that reduces accuracy; more repeats will not fix it.
options.C: This is a systematic error that reduces precision only.
options.D: This is a mistake, so the data are invalid and must be discarded.

questions.explanation: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is systematic. It moves the results away from the true value (accuracy), and averaging repeats cannot remove it; the thermometer must be calibrated or replaced. Option A describes random error, which scatters results both ways.
